manifest.name: UNO English Pathfinder Machine-Readable Specification
manifest.source: UNO English Pathfinder Question Bank v1.3
principles: territory is separate from curricular home
professional intent is separate from intellectual profile
results are never gated by contact information
same rules should support GitHub and future QSF implementations

multi_select.rule: If two options are selected, combine vectors then normalize to the same total module score budget as a single selection.

LANG.name: Language
LANG.description: Structure, variation, accents/dialects, language change, discourse.

LIT.name: Literature
LIT.description: Close reading, genre, literary history, interpretation.

CUL.name: Culture & Identity
CUL.description: History, race/ethnicity, gender, migration, power, popular/visual culture.

CRA.name: Creative Craft
CRA.description: Fact-based storytelling, voice, form, scene, style.

RHE.name: Rhetoric & Persuasion
RHE.description: Audience, argument, discourse, how communication accomplishes things.

MLT.name: Multilingualism
MLT.description: Language learning, bilingualism, cross-linguistic experience, intercultural communication.

EDP.name: Editing & Publishing
EDP.description: Revision, selection, shaping texts, publication processes.

PRO.name: Professional Communication
PRO.description: Clarity, usability, information design, audience-centered communication.

INQ.name: Inquiry & Analysis
INQ.description: Evidence, patterns, research questions, independent investigation.

questions.title: What brings you into our corner of the university?
questions.prompt: First, what brings you into our corner of the university?

options.text: 🌱 I could see English becoming a big part of my undergraduate degree.
🧩 I'd like to add more English to what I'm already studying.
🎓 I'm looking beyond the bachelor's degree.
➕ I'm already a graduate student somewhere else.
🧭 I have absolutely no idea yet. That's why I clicked this thing.

questions.purpose: Soft credential/commitment routing only; no intellectual score.

questions.title: Free afternoon
questions.prompt: Someone unexpectedly gives you an afternoon with nothing due. Which rabbit hole could actually steal two hours from you?

options.text: 🗣️ Why does everybody around here pronounce that differently?
📚 A book sends me down a historical rabbit hole.
✍️ Something happened this morning that would make a great story.
💬 An argument online makes me fascinated by how it is persuading people.
🌎 I hear someone switching between languages and wonder what is happening.

questions.title: Pick a rabbit hole
questions.prompt: You've got 20 minutes to disappear down an internet rabbit hole. Pick up to two.

options.text: 🗣️ Why people have different accents
📜 A bizarre moment in history
🧠 How bilingual brains handle two languages
✍️ How a great writer pulled off that sentence
📱 Why everyone suddenly talks about something the same way
📰 How something goes from draft to published

questions.title: Oddly satisfying
questions.prompt: Which sounds most oddly satisfying?

options.text: ✂️ Cutting 200 unnecessary words
🔍 Finding a pattern nobody noticed
🧩 Making something complicated make sense
📚 Realizing two wildly different books are secretly talking to each other
🗣️ Hearing an accent and wondering where it came from
✍️ Getting one paragraph exactly right

questions.title: Fix one thing
questions.prompt: Which of these would bother you enough that you'd actually want to fix it?

options.text: 📝 Instructions that somehow make a simple task impossible. Please. Give them to me.
✍️ A fascinating story told badly. There's something good in there.
🎓 Someone who understands something but cannot explain it to students.
📖 An interpretation of a book that completely ignores its historical context.
🗣️ Someone saying another person's way of speaking is “wrong.”

questions.title: Choose your superpower
questions.prompt: You get one suspiciously specific superpower. Keep one.

options.text: 🎯 Know exactly what an audience needs to hear
🧠 See the hidden mental process behind language
📚 See every text in its historical and cultural web
✍️ Turn lived experience into a story people cannot stop reading
👩‍🏫 Find the explanation that finally makes something click
🔎 Spot the evidence everyone else missed

questions.purpose: Clean forced-choice discriminator; one answer alone can never establish confidence.

questions.title: Language gets interesting when...
questions.prompt: Language gets weirdest - and most interesting - when...

options.text: 🧠 ...it meets the mind. How do we understand words so quickly? What happens with multiple languages?
👥 ...it meets society. Accents, dialects, identity, judgment, change.
🌎 ...languages meet each other. Learning, mixing, switching, moving between languages.
📝 ...it becomes text. Why does one wording work better for an audience?
🔬 ...someone realizes we can collect data about all of this.

questions.title: I don't have an accent.
questions.prompt: Someone says: “I don't have an accent.” Your brain:

options.text: 😂 Oh, you absolutely do.
🗺️ Okay, but where did you grow up?
👥 Interesting that some accents get noticed and others do not.
🔬 Can I record you? For science.
😌 My brain has no response to this information.

questions.purpose: Sociolinguistic/phonetic orientation with a zero-point fun option.

questions.title: Two languages, one mind
questions.prompt: A bilingual speaker knows the word they want - but the other language gets there first. What makes you curious?

options.text: 🧠 What just happened in their mind?
🌎 When and why does one language become easier to access than another?
👥 Would this change depending on who they are talking to?
🎓 How does this affect learning or teaching another language?
✍️ How could a writer represent that multilingual experience on the page?

questions.title: The mystery phrase
questions.prompt: A phrase suddenly seems to be everywhere - except among people twenty years older. You get one question answered.

options.text: 🧭 Where did it come from?
👥 Why did this group adopt it?
📈 How is its meaning changing?
⚖️ Why do some people hate hearing it?
🧠 How does a brain learn a new meaning for an old word?

questions.title: Linguistic detective
questions.prompt: Pick your evidence. Up to two.

options.text: 🎙️ Recordings
💬 Conversations
🧠 Experiments
📱 Social media
📝 Written texts
🌎 Multilingual speakers

questions.title: Words doing things
questions.prompt: Two messages contain the same basic information, but one persuades people and the other falls flat. What do you want to know?

options.text: 🎯 Who each message imagined its audience to be
🧱 How the argument was structured
🗣️ Which wording choices changed the effect
🌎 What cultural assumptions the messages relied on
🧪 How we could test which version actually works

questions.title: The unfamiliar text
questions.prompt: A professor puts an unfamiliar text in front of you. What is most likely to make you lean forward?

options.text: 🔍 Something strange is happening in the writing itself. I want to work out what it is doing.
🕰️ This text came from another world. I want the history and culture around it.
🌍 Whose perspective are we getting - and whose are we not?
🔗 It reminds me of something happening now.
✍️ I am noticing techniques I could steal. Respectfully.

questions.title: The old book
questions.prompt: You find a 150-year-old book with somebody's notes in the margins. What is most interesting?

options.text: 📖 The book
✏️ The notes
🕰️ The person who wrote the notes
🌎 The world they were living in
👀 Why am I being forced to choose?

questions.title: Whose story?
questions.prompt: A story is celebrated as “universal.” What question are you most tempted to ask?

options.text: 🌎 Universal for whom?
🗣️ Whose voice sounds “normal” in this story?
🕰️ Would readers in another time have seen it that way?
🔍 What in the text makes people read it as universal?
✍️ How would the story change if somebody else told it?

questions.purpose: Identity, perspective, historical reception, textual analysis.

questions.title: Borrow a time machine
questions.prompt: You get ONE literary field trip.

options.text: 🏰 Medieval world
🎭 Shakespeare's London
🕯️ Nineteenth century
🗽 Twentieth-century America
🌎 Somewhere shaped by colonialism and its aftermath
🚀 Actually, take me back to the present

questions.purpose: Low-weight flavor question for course/faculty hooks.

questions.title: The family story
questions.prompt: You learn something remarkable about someone in your family. Nobody agrees on exactly what happened. What pulls you in?

options.text: ✍️ I can already see the opening scene.
🎙️ Start interviewing everybody before their versions disappear.
🗃️ Find letters, photographs, records - what actually happened?
🌎 Zoom out: what does this tell us about their time, place, or community?
🧠 Why do people remember the same event differently?

graduate_variant.prompt: You inherit an archive of contradictory accounts around one life/event. What becomes the project?

questions.title: I have a story about that.
questions.prompt: “I have a story about that.” Your reaction:

options.text: ✍️ Tell it.
🔍 Research it.
🎙️ Interview someone.
🧠 Figure out why you remember it that way.
😬 Maybe take that one to the grave.

questions.purpose: Fast CNF orientation with a breathing-room answer.

questions.title: Truth gets messy
questions.prompt: You are writing about a real event, and the facts resist the neat version of the story. What sounds most interesting?

options.text: 🧭 Let the messiness become part of the form.
🔎 Keep digging until I understand the contradictions.
🎙️ Put different people's versions into conversation.
⚖️ Think hard about what I owe the real people in the story.
✂️ Find the clearest truthful version without flattening it.

questions.title: The broken draft
questions.prompt: Someone sends you a draft and says, “Something isn't working.” What sounds satisfying?

options.text: ✂️ Find the sentence doing absolutely nothing and delete it.
🧭 Figure out what the piece is really trying to become.
👀 Think about the reader: where will they get confused, bored, persuaded, surprised?
📰 Think beyond the draft: where does this belong and how do we get it to readers?
🏃 Pretend I never received the file.

questions.title: Hit publish
questions.prompt: What is the most satisfying moment?

options.text: ✍️ Writing it
✂️ Making it better
📰 Choosing what gets published
🎨 Figuring out how readers experience it
🚀 Sending it into the world

questions.title: Your nemesis appears: ASSEMBLY REQUIRED
questions.prompt: The instructions are terrible. You:

options.text: 🛠️ Rewrite them.
🖼️ Add visuals.
🧪 Watch someone try them and see where they fail.
🤬 Complain about them while assembling it incorrectly.

questions.title: The audience problem
questions.prompt: You have one complicated idea and three audiences: experts, new students, and the public. What sounds fun?

options.text: 🎯 Rebuild the explanation for each audience.
🧩 Find the one analogy that works across all three.
📐 Decide what each audience needs first, second, and never.
🧪 Test versions and see what people actually understand.
✍️ Make all three versions sound good, not merely correct.

graduate_variant.prompt: A team hands you a substantial project and says: We know what we mean; we do not know how to communicate it.

questions.title: Make this usable
questions.prompt: A page is technically accurate but nobody can use it. Pick up to two things you want to fix first.

options.text: 🧭 Organization
✂️ Wordiness
🎨 Visual hierarchy
🎯 Audience mismatch
🧪 Whether users can actually complete the task

questions.title: Imagine you discover you love teaching
questions.prompt: Imagine you discover that you actually love teaching. Where can you picture yourself?

options.text: 🏫 An English classroom: literature, writing, language - middle or high school.
🌎 A multilingual classroom: helping people develop English while learning how languages work.
🧠 Somewhere people are figuring things out: tutoring, mentoring, maybe college.
🔬 Wait - can I study learning instead? I am as interested in how people acquire/use language as teaching it.
😅 You lost me at “discover that you love teaching.” Respectfully, no.

questions.purpose: Distinguish Secondary English, TESOL, pedagogy, and language research.

questions.title: They still don't get it
questions.prompt: You've explained something twice. They still don't get it.

options.text: 🔄 Explain it differently.
🧩 Break it into pieces.
👂 Ask what part is not clicking.
🔍 Become fascinated by why it is not clicking.
🏃 I was not built for this scenario.

questions.title: Study learning instead
questions.prompt: Suppose you could spend a semester studying one learning mystery. Which one?

options.text: 🌎 Why some ways of learning another language work better than others
🧠 How people process and retrieve language in real time
✍️ How writers learn through feedback and revision
👥 How classroom identities and communities shape participation
📚 How people learn to interpret difficult texts

questions.title: Choose an artifact
questions.prompt: You have to investigate ONE ordinary thing as if it were an artifact from another civilization. Pick it.

options.text: 📱 A week of TikToks
📣 An advertisement
👗 A fashion trend
🎵 A song everyone suddenly knows
🗣️ A phrase people your age use that older people do not
📖 A bestselling novel

questions.purpose: Wildcard; choice lightly scores, follow-up does the diagnostic work.

questions.title: Academic dinner party
questions.prompt: You arrive late. One seat is left at each table. Where are you sitting?

options.text: 📚 People arguing about what a famous book actually means
🗣️ People comparing accents and telling language stories
✍️ People swapping unbelievable true stories
🧠 People debating how language works in the mind
🛠️ People redesigning the menu because apparently that became the evening project
😈 The table with the best gossip. Obviously.

questions.title: One question forever
questions.prompt: You can keep asking ONE kind of question for the rest of your academic life. Which sounds least exhausting?

options.text: 🔍 What is really going on here?
🌎 How did culture/history/power shape this?
🗣️ Why do people use language this way?
📚 What else can this text mean?
✍️ How can I make this truer, sharper, or more alive on the page?
🎯 How can I make this work better for the people who need it?
🎓 How can I help someone else understand this?

graduate_variant.prompt: You receive protected time to pursue one family of questions for a year. Which sounds least exhausting?

questions.title: You keep coming back to language...
questions.prompt: Okay, which mystery would you steal an answer to?

options.text: 🧠 How can two languages coexist in one mind?
👥 Why do people change how they speak around different people?
🌎 What actually happens while someone learns another language?
🎙️ What makes an accent sound like that?
📈 How does a new way of speaking spread?
💬 How does wording change what people believe?

questions.title: Okay, the story got complicated.
questions.prompt: Your sources disagree. Good news or bad news?

options.text: ✨ Good news. That disagreement is part of the story.
🔎 Bad news. I need to establish what happened.
🧠 Interesting news. Why do they remember it differently?
⚖️ Complicated news. What can I responsibly say about real people?

questions.title: You are not done with that text yet.
questions.prompt: What pulls you further in?

options.text: 🕰️ The historical world around it
🔍 The writer's formal choices
🌎 Gender, race, class, empire, or social expectations
👥 What readers at the time thought
🔗 How we would read it differently now

questions.title: Apparently unusable information bothers you.
questions.prompt: Which part of “make it better” sounds best?

options.text: 🎯 Understand the audience
🧭 Restructure the information
✂️ Edit the language
🎨 Redesign how people encounter it
🧪 Test it with real users

questions.title: Teaching keeps sneaking into your answers...
questions.prompt: What is the satisfying part?

options.text: 💡 The moment something clicks
🧩 Designing a better way to explain it
👂 Learning how another person thinks
🌎 Working across languages/cultures
🔬 Studying why learning succeeds or fails

questions.title: Okay. What do you want to know about it?
questions.prompt: Okay. What do you want to know about it?

options.text: 🕰️ Where it came from and how it got here
🎯 Who it is trying to reach or persuade
🌎 What it says about identity, culture, or power
🗣️ How its language is changing or doing social work
🔍 How its form/structure makes it work
📣 Why people keep sharing, reading, or repeating it

questions.purpose: Wildcard follow-up; turns artifact choice into a diagnostic orientation.

questions.title: Pick a setting
questions.prompt: Where would you most happily spend an hour?

options.text: ☕ Coffee shop with a notebook
📚 Library stacks
🎙️ Language lab
📰 Editorial room
🏫 Classroom
🌳 Somewhere outside with something to read

questions.title: Pick your evidence aesthetic
questions.prompt: Which pile on a desk looks most irresistible?

options.text: 📜 Old letters and marginal notes
🎧 Headphones + waveforms
📝 A draft covered in edits
📊 A tiny dataset begging for a pattern
📚 Three books that should not belong together but somehow do

combinations.copy: Language Studies + TESOL may be worth exploring together.
An English minor and TESOL may fit the same language-focused curiosity; advising can explain the curricular mechanics.
Secondary English Teaching and TESOL connect around teaching, but they are distinct credentials with different professional purposes.
The MA and a graduate certificate may be worth discussing together; do not imply the certificate requires the MA.

solas_lab.title: SoLaS Lab
solas_lab.copy: A place to explore language curiosities through sociolinguistics and language-structure research.

linden_review.title: The Linden Review
linden_review.copy: Explore editing and publishing experience connected to Creative Nonfiction.

writing_center.title: UNO Writing Center
writing_center.copy: A writing and mentoring environment that may appeal to visitors drawn to teaching, feedback, and composition.

graduate_ta.title: English Graduate Teaching Assistantships
graduate_ta.copy: Eligible English graduate degree and certificate students can explore competitive Teaching Assistantships; check the current page for duties, deadlines, compensation, and eligibility.

callbacks.record_for_science: We had a feeling after “Can I record you? For science.” 🎙️
callbacks.marginalia: You picked the marginalia over the book. We haven't forgotten.
callbacks.assembly_haunting: Those assembly instructions are apparently still haunting you.
callbacks.take_to_grave: We are respectfully not asking about the story you chose to take to the grave.
callbacks.gossip_table: For the record, choosing the gossip table told us almost nothing academically. Excellent choice.

confidence.CONFIDENT: We're seeing a pretty clear pattern...
confidence.MIXED: Your answers keep refusing to stay in one lane. That is useful information.
confidence.AMBIGUOUS: You're making this difficult. We like that.
confidence.INSUFFICIENT: You're harder to read than we expected. In fairness, several of your choices were gloriously unhelpful. Academically? We have almost nothing. Spiritually? Immaculate. Give us three actual answers and we'll take another shot.

profile_shape.BROAD: Apparently the problem is that English contains too many things you like. Your answers spread across the department rather than forming one obvious winner.
profile_shape.EXPLORATORY: You're still exploring - and your answers actually look like it. Nothing is dominating yet, so we're not going to pretend one path is ‘the answer.’

bonus.invite: Think we've got you wrong? Challenge the result.
bonus.CONFIRM: You made us check. The pattern held.

community.heading: Want to stay connected to English?
community.body: Leave your email and we can send you relevant English opportunities, events, resources, or ways to explore the parts of English that caught your attention.
